title: Who Is Shailesh Jejurikar? The Mumbai Boy Who Shared a Classroom With Satya Nadella — and Now Runs a $380 Billion American Giant

body:
When Procter & Gamble named Shailesh Jejurikar its president and CEO effective January 1, 2026, the announcement did more than shuffle a corporate org chart. It placed an Indian-born, IIM-educated executive at the helm of one of America’s oldest and most iconic consumer goods empires — a company that has been in continuous operation for 187 years and touches the daily routines of roughly five billion people worldwide.

Jejurikar, 58, is the first Asian-born CEO in P&G’s history, and only the second non-American to hold the title. The first was Dutchman Durk Jager, who lasted barely 17 months in the job back in 1998. Jejurikar’s appointment puts him in the same rarefied company as Satya Nadella at Microsoft, Sundar Pichai at Alphabet, and Arvind Krishna at IBM — Indians who lead companies that define American business.

A Bombay Kid in Hyderabad

Jejurikar was born in Mumbai to a Maharashtrian father and a Gujarati mother. From Class 8, he boarded at Hyderabad Public School, where he became head boy and played competitive cricket for Hyderabad’s under-17 team. His seatmate during those years? A quiet, bookish kid named Satya Nadella. The two have stayed close friends ever since — a detail that now reads like a footnote written by destiny, given that one runs the world’s most valuable software company and the other runs its largest consumer goods maker.

“The key to business growth? First believing it’s possible,” Jejurikar has said in interviews, reflecting on a philosophy he traces back to those formative years in India. He earned his BA in Economics from Elphinstone College, Mumbai, and then his MBA from IIM Lucknow — one of India’s most competitive business schools — before joining P&G as an assistant brand manager in 1989.

Thirty-Seven Years, One Company

"“The need to accelerate investment in growth accelerated the need on productivity.” — Shailesh Jejurikar, on P&G’s restructuring strategy Sundar Pichai."

In an era of serial job-hopping and founder-CEO cults, Jejurikar’s career is almost quaint: 37 years at a single company, rising from assistant brand manager in India to the global corner office. But calling it a straight line would be misleading. His path wound through Kenya, Singapore, the Philippines, Korea, and North America, building businesses across health care, beauty, and home care before he found his groove in fabric care — the division that houses Tide, Ariel, Downy, and Febreze, and accounts for nearly a third of P&G’s total sales.

By 2019, he ran the entire Global Fabric & Home Care sector, P&G’s largest and most profitable unit. In 2021, he was elevated to Chief Operating Officer, overseeing the sprawling Enterprise Markets that span Latin America, India, the Middle East, Africa, and Southeast Asia — plus the company’s IT, supply chain, and global business services. It was, in retrospect, a clear audition for the top job.

“The need to accelerate investment in growth accelerated the need on productivity.” — Shailesh Jejurikar, on P&G’s restructuring strategy

Running the Show in Turbulent Times

Jejurikar didn’t inherit a victory lap. He stepped into the CEO chair amid a global slowdown in consumer spending, trade war tremors from the conflict in Iran, and a company-wide restructuring that will eliminate 7,000 office jobs over two years. P&G has already spent $782 million on separation packages and asset write-downs, and has exited operations in Bangladesh and Pakistan.

But the early signals are promising. In its most recent quarter (January–March 2026), P&G posted organic sales growth of 3 percent, with all ten product categories and all global regions growing. One of Jejurikar’s signature moves has been a premium innovation push in China, where the company launched “Pampers Prestige” — diapers woven with real silk fibers, drawing on China’s centuries-old reverence for the material. The bet is working: P&G’s baby care business in Greater China has gained nearly 3 percent market share, even as the country’s birth rate hits record lows.

P&G is set to report its full fiscal year 2026 results on July 29, with Wall Street expecting roughly $87 billion in revenue and a $16.6 billion profit. For Jejurikar, it will be the first annual report card of his tenure as CEO — and investors are watching closely.

A Family of Leaders

The Jejurikar story extends beyond one corner office. Shailesh’s elder brother, Rajesh Jejurikar, serves as Executive Director and CEO of the Auto and Farm Sector at Mahindra & Mahindra, one of India’s most storied industrial conglomerates. Between them, the brothers lead companies with a combined market capitalization north of $400 billion — one anchored in the American heartland, the other rooted in India’s industrial future.

“It is a proud moment for India and the family,” Rajesh said when his brother’s appointment was announced. Shailesh’s wife, Sankhya, is a visual artist. They have two sons, Shashank and Siddharth, and live in the Cincinnati area where P&G has been headquartered since 1837.

What He Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, Jejurikar’s rise carries a particular resonance. He didn’t arrive in America as a startup founder or a tech prodigy. He arrived as a brand manager — a cog in a very large machine — and spent nearly four decades earning his way to the top through the kind of patient, unglamorous excellence that rarely makes headlines but quietly reshapes institutions.

In a landscape where Indian-origin CEOs increasingly dominate American technology, Jejurikar’s appointment extends that influence into consumer goods — into the laundry rooms and bathrooms and nurseries of ordinary households everywhere. When you reach for a bottle of Tide, a pack of Gillette razors, or a tube of Olay, the company behind those products is now led by a man who once bowled medium pace for Hyderabad’s under-17 cricket team and dreamed big at a boarding school in the Deccan.

That, in the end, may be the most Indian thing about him: the belief that showing up, every single day, for 37 years, is its own kind of greatness.
